opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I can't speak for DJI, and I don't have any inside knowledge of how they make decisions. But looking at how they've built the company over the years, I can guess at the logic they'd probably use.

First, I think they'd ask whether there's a real product with a clear user need, not just "robotics" as a buzzword. DJI didn't win by being the first drone company. They won because they made something that a photographer, a filmmaker, or a farmer could take out of the box and use reliably. So the question wouldn't be "should we do humanoids because everyone's talking about humanoids." It would be "is there a specific task where a robot can deliver value today, at a price people will pay, with reliability people can trust?"

Second, they'd look at where their existing strengths carry over. And a lot of them do: motors, gimbals and stabilization, sensors, perception, embedded compute, battery management, and above all supply chain and manufacturing at scale in Shenzhen. If a robotics category leans heavily on those things, that's an unfair advantage. If it mostly depends on something they don't have, like a big breakthrough in general-purpose manipulation or foundation models for embodied AI, then the edge is much smaller and the risk is much higher.

Third, timing. DJI has historically been good at entering when the technology is just mature enough to make a consumer-grade product that works, not years early when it only works in demos. In robotics there's a lot of excitement right now, but there's still a big gap between a great video and a product that runs ten thousand hours in someone's home or factory without failing. I think a company like that would be patient and wait for the point where engineering, not research, is the bottleneck, because engineering is where they excel.

And you can already see hints of this in adjacent areas: education robots, robotic lawn mowers, stabilizers, agricultural drones. Those are kind of robotics already, just in narrow forms. So my guess is they wouldn't make a single dramatic "we're entering robotics" announcement. They'd expand outward step by step from what they already do well, into categories where the hardware advantage matters and the use case is concrete.

r001.rationale: The response recommends finding a concrete user need, but does not say DJI should identify needs within its existing user base.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because DJI is probably the closest thing we have to a case study of how a hardware company actually makes these calls.

The first thing to understand is that DJI doesn't really ask "should we enter robotics" as an abstract strategy question. The way the company thinks is much more bottom-up. It starts from the technology stack they already own. A drone is, in a sense, already a robot. You have perception, you have state estimation, you have motor control, you have real-time embedded compute, you have a supply chain that can produce millions of units at consistent quality. So the internal question is less "is robotics a good market" and more "where does our existing stack give us an unfair advantage, and where would we be starting from zero."

The second thing is that DJI is very disciplined about product definition. Frank Wang's culture has always been about finding a product where the technology is just mature enough that you can deliver something that clearly works, and the user experience is so obviously better than the alternative that it sells itself. Phantom did that. Osmo did that. Ronin did that. So when they look at robotics, I think they'd be asking: is there a specific form factor where we can hit that bar today? Not a research platform, not a demo, but a product a normal person or a normal business can buy and have it just work. If the honest answer is "not yet," they'll wait. RoboMaster is a good example of that. It's partly education, partly a way to grow talent and keep the robotics muscle warm, without betting the company on a product category that isn't ready.

Third, they'd look at cost structure. DJI wins when they can drive the bill of materials down and the volume up at the same time. Humanoids today are the opposite. The costs are high, the volumes are low, and the use cases are still being argued about. That's not a DJI-shaped problem yet. Something like autonomous agricultural robots, or industrial inspection, or logistics in constrained environments, those look a lot more DJI-shaped, because they can reuse their perception and flight control heritage and the customer already has a measurable return.

And finally, there's the question of what the company is good at versus what the market is excited about. DJI has historically been willing to ignore hype. They were late to a lot of things people demanded, and it usually turned out fine. So my guess is they'd approach robotics by picking one or two narrow verticals where their stack transfers almost directly, build a product that's clearly the best in that niche, and let that teach them what the next step is. That's how they've grown every other time. I'd be surprised if they did it differently here.

r001.rationale: The response discusses finding robotics niches that fit DJI’s technology and have measurable customer returns, but it does not propose assessing needs within DJI’s existing user base.

astra-6.text:
I think DJI would start by asking, where do we have a real technical advantage, and does that advantage solve a problem people will pay for? A drone already combines sensing, control, planning, and hardware, so there’s a natural connection to robotics. But that doesn’t mean every robotics market is a good fit.

The harder question is the application. Can you define a task clearly enough, make the robot reliable, and deliver it at a price that makes sense? Then you have to look at manufacturing, distribution, and service—not just whether you can build an impressive prototype.

So my guess is they’d look for a focused use case where their existing capabilities give them an advantage. I wouldn’t assume they’d enter robotics simply because it’s an exciting category.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on technical advantage, customer willingness to pay, and finding a focused use case, but it does not propose identifying needs within DJI’s existing user base.

sol-6.1.text:
I think DJI would probably start by asking, what can we do uniquely well, and where does that solve a real customer problem? They have experience combining hardware, software, sensing, and control into a product that people can actually use. Those capabilities are relevant to robotics, but that alone doesn’t tell you which robot to build.

The next question would be the application. Who is the customer? What task are they trying to accomplish? How reliably does the robot need to perform, and can you deliver that at a price that makes sense? A compelling demo is one thing; a product that works every day is another.

So my guess is they would look for a fairly specific entry point where their existing capabilities give them an advantage, prove the product and the economics, and expand from there. I wouldn’t assume they would start with the broad goal of entering robotics. They might start with a problem worth solving, and the answer happens to be a robot.

r001.rationale: The response recommends identifying a customer problem and application, but it does not say DJI should look for needs among its existing user base.
